cards.title: Purpose brand: own a job, not a category
cards.summary: Integrate the brand around one clear Job to Be Done so customers think of you automatically, instead of becoming a price-competing category placeholder.
cards.use_when: Deciding brand positioning or evaluating whether feature/benefit expansion is diluting what the brand stands for
steps: Identify the specific job the brand is associated with and check whether it has become the default answer in customers' minds (the source notes strong brands like Google and Starbucks became verbs for their job and were built with minimal advertising).

Recognize the failure mode: brands that don't integrate around a job become category placeholders forced to compete on price with look-alike competitors (source cites airlines, automakers, business hotel chains, rental cars, PC clones).
Use the purpose brand as an internal filter: a clear job makes explicit which features and improvements are relevant and which are irrelevant, guiding product, marketing and advertising decisions.
Treat it as an economic asset: the source argues purpose brands create differentiation, premium pricing and growth potential.
Watch for erosion when the company chases 'news' or price justification through added benefits rather than deepening the job.
caveats: Brand status is hard to regain once lost; the source treats Volvo's post-1999 shift toward flashier cars as a cautionary case where a safety purpose brand weakened and recovery was slow.
The 'ultimate competitive advantage' framing is the source's strong claim, not a guaranteed outcome.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Write a job spec before designing the solution
cards.summary: Capture the full richness of the customer's job in a job spec covering functional, emotional and social dimensions, tradeoffs, competitors and anxieties, then use it as the innovation blueprint.
cards.use_when: After customer research has surfaced a job and you need to translate it into requirements for a product, service or experience
steps: Document the functional, emotional and social dimensions that define the desired progress the customer wants.
Record the tradeoffs the customer is willing to make (what they will accept or give up to get the job done).
List the full set of competing solutions that must be beaten, not just direct product competitors.
Identify the obstacles and anxieties that must be overcome for the customer to switch or to succeed with the solution.
Treat the job spec as the blueprint for innovation: it should be detailed enough to guide design of the product and of the purchase and use experiences.
caveats: A job is rich and complex; a thin or purely functional spec will produce a solution that misses what customers actually need.
The source insists solutions must be complete, meaning core product plus purchase and use experiences; a good product alone is not enough.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Treat every complete solution as a service
cards.summary: Even product companies must design the full experience of purchase and use, because a complete solution to a job always functions like a service.
cards.use_when: When your product is strong but customers still struggle to buy, onboard or get value from it
steps: Map the customer's end-to-end experience of buying and using your offering, not just the product itself.
Identify obstacles or anxieties at each step that could stop the customer from hiring you or from firing their current solution.
Design deliberate experiences that remove those obstacles, since the source argues all successful job solutions ultimately behave like services even for product companies.
Check for misalignment: the purchase and use experience must match what the job spec requires, not what is convenient for internal functions.
caveats: This is a design principle, not a claim that every company must literally sell a subscription or service.
The source's examples come from healthcare, automotive and education; the transfer to ecommerce is that checkout, delivery, onboarding and support all count as part of the solution.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Integrate processes around the job, not the org chart
cards.summary: Competitive advantage comes from proprietary cross-functional processes that deliver the customer's job, and large reorganizations usually fail to create that value.
cards.use_when: When restructuring seems like the answer to growth or execution problems, or when functions deliver in silos
steps: Before reorganizing, ask how different parts of the organization interact to systematically deliver the offering that performs the customer's job; that is what matters more than reporting lines.
Note the source's evidence: a 2010 Bain study found fewer than one-third of major reorganizations delivered material improvement, and many destroyed value.
Look for the missing role: in most companies nobody owns understanding and delivering the customer's job, so assign stewardship of the job.
Deliberately define new processes and coordination mechanisms where functions are usually siloed.
Accept that traditional structures and functions will persist, so move toward job-centricity through processes, metrics and culture rather than a single sweeping reorg.
caveats: The source explicitly says large-scale reorgs are usually not practical and traditional structures have value; this is not a call to abolish functions.
Building job-centered processes is described as very hard and slow, not a quick fix.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Shift complexity from the customer to your processes
cards.summary: Job-aligned processes should absorb the nuisance work customers would otherwise do themselves, leaving them with positive experience and progress.
cards.use_when: When customers abandon or stall because of friction such as paperwork, coordination or repeated follow-up
steps: Identify the steps where the customer currently carries complexity (finding information, chasing documents, coordinating multiple parties, navigating policies).
Redesign internal processes so the vendor takes on that work instead of the customer.

Use SNHU as the example: it moved from mailing packages and waiting weeks for the prospect to follow up, to tracking response time in minutes with a goal of calling back in under ten minutes, asking permission on the call to chase transcripts, and paying the transcript fee itself.
Measure the outcome the customer cares about (how quickly they get a decision and complete information) rather than the volume of internal activity like packages sent.
caveats: The SNHU results are a case example, not a guaranteed return for other businesses.
Removing customer complexity usually raises internal cost and process intensity; the source argues this pays off through acquisition and premium pricing, but that tradeoff should be tested.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Measure customer-benefit metrics, not internal activity
cards.summary: Replace internal financial and activity metrics with externally relevant measures of whether the customer's job got done.
cards.use_when: When dashboards full of conversion, retention or cost metrics don't explain whether customers are actually succeeding
steps: Define metrics that track the customer benefit tied to the specific job, and use them to steer processes.

Use the source's examples as patterns: SNHU tracks minutes to respond to an inquiry; Amazon tracks when orders are delivered, not when they are shipped; Intuit builds a unique metric set per product tied to the specific benefit delivered.
Ask questions like: how much time did we save this customer, did we spare them work they didn't want to do, did we improve their cash flow.
Recognize that the right metrics often don't fall out of existing systems; Intuit reports interpolating survey and server data to estimate things like labor hours avoided.
Treat the right job spec as the origin of the right processes, which in turn generate the right data for judging performance.
caveats: Internal revenue metrics can mislead: the source describes Intuit forcing trial users to register by phone to enable upsells, which created friction and focused people on revenue rather than the customer benefit.
Customer-benefit measurement is described as genuinely hard and not automatically available from systems.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Process optimization needs a job-alignment factor
cards.summary: Efficiency alone can make you better at the wrong things; optimize processes for efficiency and alignment with the customer's job.
cards.use_when: When process improvement, automation or cost reduction is underway and you need a criterion beyond throughput
steps: Add an explicit job-alignment check to any optimization effort: does this change improve delivery of the customer's job?
Remember the source's warning that optimizing an unaligned process means getting better and better at doing the wrong thing.
Use Amazon as the pattern: it starts from the customer and the metrics that matter for the customer, and works backward to processes for vast selection, low prices and fast delivery.
Accept ambidexterity: processes should be both efficient and flexible, because how you solve a job changes over time even though the job itself is stable.
Stay attached to the job, not to today's solution, so you don't bend the definition of the job to fit the process.
caveats: The source's point is that textbook process optimization is insufficient, not that efficiency is unimportant.
Flexibility has costs; the claim is that job attachment justifies them when the job is well understood.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Use subroutines to make process reuse deliberate
cards.summary: Instead of informally sharing best practices, identify repeatable process modules that can be reused wherever the same operation is needed.
cards.use_when: When scaling operations across regions, product lines or channels and each team reinvents the same steps
steps: For each process step, ask whether this process or subroutine is likely to be needed in other activities.
Treat the organization as a collection of processes, each a string of subroutines, some custom and some modular imports, aligned to the customer's job.
Keep some pieces persistent and let others change over time, mirroring the programming use of subroutines that reduce development and maintenance cost while improving quality and reliability.
Use the Amazon model of shared platform, technology and guiding principles across businesses so teams can move fast.
caveats: The source presents this as a principle imported from software engineering, illustrated by Amazon, not as a universal implementation recipe.
Modular reuse can conflict with local adaptation; the alignment with the job is the tie-breaker.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Start every innovation from the job-spec press release
cards.summary: Frame a new offering by writing the customer-facing announcement first, so experience and process decisions derive from the job it will be hired to do.
cards.use_when: Kicking off a new product, feature or service, especially when engineering or channel ownership is fragmented
steps: Write a mock press release describing what the customer will be able to accomplish and the job the product is hired for.
Present it to everyone whose work will contribute to fulfilling that job, including engineers, analysts and marketing, not just the product owner.
Derive all experiences and processes from the clarity of that stated job, and keep the group aligned even if different people own different pieces of the product.
Treat Amazon's use of this practice as the source's example of starting from the customer and designing backward.
caveats: The press release is a framing device, not a substitute for customer research into the job.
The source does not describe the full Amazon document or approval process; treat details beyond the framing as outside the source.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Give the customer's job an internal owner
cards.summary: Assign stewardship of end-to-end job delivery, because functions and product lines rarely have anyone accountable for the customer's job.
cards.use_when: When customers experience a broken journey across handoffs and each function believes it is doing its job
steps: Check whether any role is responsible for understanding and consistently delivering the customer's job across functions.
Use the intensive care example: post-surgical patients died because the critical-care job had no owner in any existing medical function, until Dwight Harken created the concept and the ICU.

Empower a process owner over a job-facing sequence, following the Mayo Clinic pattern where one person takes charge of coordinating specialties, data and sequencing for the visit, with specialists keeping open slots for real-time needs.
Ask the diagnostic question Harken asked: everyone is doing what they are supposed to and all processes work as designed, so why is the customer outcome still failing?
caveats: This does not require a full reorganization; the source says stewardship can be achieved through processes, metrics and culture.
The Mayo and ICU cases are healthcare examples; in ecommerce the transferable idea is owning the end-to-end job journey across teams.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Run meetings focused on the job to avoid politics
cards.summary: A recurring cross-functional forum centered on the customer's job gives diverse specialists a shared language and prevents debate from collapsing into opinions and turf.
cards.use_when: When cross-functional teams argue from their own professional backgrounds instead of solving the customer's problem
steps: Convene senior staff from across the organization regularly, as the source describes the CFPB's policy committee doing weekly for two hours.
Direct the entire conversation to one job to be done and what tools will be used over time to address it.
Invite each participant to bring their expertise and opinions on solving that job, rather than defending their function's mission.

Design the organization so groups with potentially conflicting past-focused and future-focused missions share a division and a job, as the source describes merging enforcement with supervision, and research with markets and regulation.
Use the job as the rallying cause: if you don't focus on a job, the source says people focus on their scars and politics.
caveats: This is drawn from the CFPB setup under Elizabeth Warren, a regulatory context; the transferable mechanism is the job-focused meeting, not the specific divisional structure.
The source warns of a typical DC paralysis risk that the job focus was designed to avoid.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Beware stack fallacy when moving into adjacent solutions
cards.summary: Technical strength in your layer does not mean you understand the customer one level up, so moving up the stack requires first-hand empathy for that customer's context.
cards.use_when: When considering a product extension or new service built on your existing technology or supply strength
steps: Check whether you have first-hand understanding of what customers one level above your current offering actually want and the context in which they use it.
Watch for the tendency to dismiss the downstream application as trivial, which the source calls stack fallacy.

Note the cautionary case: Ford and Qualcomm had deep technical capability but Wingcast, announced in 2000 for a 2003 launch, was scrapped two years later, while OnStar succeeded by focusing on the job rather than the product spec.
Import the principle outside tech: growing herbs and cooking for yourself does not prepare you to run a restaurant, and the source notes eight out of ten restaurants fail within five years.
caveats: The restaurant failure figure is the source's illustration, not a claim about your market.
The source frames stack fallacy as highlighting the same hazard as Jobs Theory, not as a rigorous predictive model.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Find the job in moments of struggle, not feature lists
cards.summary: OnStar initially bundled cool features as brochure ware, but the real job emerged only when the team listened to actual customer calls at moments of crisis.
cards.use_when: When your product has many features but customers churn because they don't need most of them
steps: Note the initial failure pattern: OnStar was a bundle of novelty features, fun at first but treated as a toy, and customers canceled because the concierge features were nice but not necessary.
Have the whole team listen directly to real customer interactions; the source describes requiring all 300 OnStar staff to spend an hour on live call-center calls.
Identify the circumstances of struggle that reveal the job: accidents, cars still moving, people screaming, and later late-night driving in unfamiliar places.

Reframe features around the job: directions became less about finding a restaurant and more about being routed through safe streets; diagnostics became about deciding what to do right now when the check-engine light comes on at 2 a.m.
Let the job explain surprising data: Chevy buyers subscribed at the same rate as Cadillac buyers because peace of mind is essential, not a luxury upgrade.
caveats: The source attributes OnStar's ultimate success to this job focus and to process innovation, not to the features it launched with.
Listening to calls is described as revealing and uncomfortable work, not a one-off survey.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Repeat time-consuming research at each execution stage
cards.summary: Features and collateral are not enough when a growing team loses touch with customer reality; direct exposure to real interactions must be repeated as the company scales.
cards.use_when: When a growing organization is making decisions from data and internal assumptions rather than customer contact
steps: Embed recurring direct customer exposure into how teams work, rather than treating it as a one-time study.

Design products and stages so internal rewards don't distort activity: the source notes that features and collateral that kept staff busy for a year didn't stop the team from lacking strong product choices at execution stage.
Notice when success in one phase (planning, collateral, sales materials) masks weakness in the next (actual product, execution).
Use the principle that understanding moments of struggle changes not only design but also how you interact with customers in those situations.
caveats: The source does not prescribe a research cadence or sample size; it argues for repeated direct exposure as the company grows.
Attribution here is the source's interpretation; it is not an experimentally validated rule.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Build process flexibility to match faster technology cycles
cards.summary: When your delivery technology iterates much faster than your host industry's validation cycle, create deliberate mid-cycle processes or you will ship outdated versions.
cards.use_when: When your product depends on rapidly improving technology embedded in a slow-moving hardware, channel or regulatory environment
steps: Diagnose the cycle mismatch: automotive development took three to five years with cars staying on the market up to ten years, while wireless technology improved faster.
Decide explicitly whether to enter at all if the standard validation rules cannot be suspended; the OnStar CEO said otherwise they'd sell eight-track tapes while others sold CDs.
Create your own mid-cycle processes and tests in cooperation with the existing validation teams, using your own staff expertise to meet the parent organization's overall quality standards.
Test across every plausible combination: different car models, windows down, pouring rain, CD player on, airbag deployed.
Recognize that even when competitors buy your technology, their slower processes may leave them a generation behind.
caveats: This required going outside the normal approval and validation sequence, described as very hard in an established organization.
The competitive advantage came from the process set as much as the product; simply owning the technology was not sufficient.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Make channel incentives a process design problem
cards.summary: A dealer or partner whose economics don't reward selling your offering can quietly kill it, so design the channel process and incentive around the job.
cards.use_when: When a partner or channel is the front line of purchase and your offering is a small share of their revenue
steps: Quantify what the partner actually earns: the source notes a dealership got a 20 percent cut of ten dollars in monthly OnStar fees, trivial compared with adding heated seats to a sale.
Expect that sales staff will avoid offerings with complicated value explanations and low commissions, so build simple explanations and account for their economics.

Anticipate the questions that derail a sale, such as whether the service is satellite or cell-phone based, whether someone always knows the driver's location, and whether someone can eavesdrop, and prepare clear answers.
Improve processes iteratively based on what you learn in the channel, rather than assuming the first design is right.
Treat service as an integrated product carried through the channel, not an add-on feature on a spec sheet.
caveats: The specific 20 percent and ten-dollar figures are from the source's OnStar example, not a general benchmark.
Channel incentives differ by market and contract structure; verify your own economics rather than copying these numbers.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Take responsibility for customer business outcomes
cards.summary: Shift from selling training modules or tools to owning the customer's transformation, and spend R&D on process innovation that shifts complexity away from the client.
cards.use_when: When your category is vulnerable to budget cuts because clients see it as a discretionary product purchase
steps: Identify the critical jobs to be done for customers, such as sales transformation rather than sales training supply.
Take responsibility for helping customers achieve their business goals, as FranklinCovey did when it moved from selling its own products to optimizing customer outcomes.
Direct R&D toward process innovation: the source reports FranklinCovey spends two-thirds of its R&D budget on process innovation to make rollout cheaper, faster and easier.

Address customer capacity constraints: Marriott could dedicate nearly ten full-time staff to a program, but most customers cannot, so designing for lighter-touch implementation becomes part of the offering.
Set expectations correctly; the source warns it is no good if clients sign up for an exercise class and discover they must climb Mount Everest.
caveats: The source reports FranklinCovey doubled revenue and increased profit tenfold over six years, but this is a case example, not a forecast for other firms.
Taking responsibility for outcomes increases scope and risk compared with selling a bounded product.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Diagnose your organization's immune system
cards.summary: Unchanged processes and local resource-allocation habits can reject a validated idea before it ships; treating process change as an immune response helps you plan for it.
cards.use_when: When a research-backed improvement keeps dying in implementation despite good evidence
steps: Trace where the idea stops: the source describes the fast-food company rejecting changes recommended to boost milkshake sales because local managers judged changes to routine processes and resource allocations too difficult.
Recognize that absence of a process is still a process; things get done chaotically and that is a warning sign, not a neutral state.
Expect that new processes introduced into an established organization are very hard, and that solutions may look impractical financially or cumbersome culturally.
Prepare for the gravitational pull of existing processes by planning coordination mechanisms, incentives and metrics before rollout.
Use jobs alignment as the criterion for whether a process should persist or change.
caveats: The milkshake example ended in a quiet death of the idea; the source uses it to show how internal forces defeat good ideas, not to claim all process changes fail.
Deming's line that if you can't describe what you are doing as a process then you don't know what you are doing is the source's framing, not an operational rule.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Use the job spec to review experiences and obstacles
cards.summary: The source's leader questions turn a job spec into an audit of whether current solutions address every detail, obstacle and stage of the customer's experience.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a product line, customer journey or growth plan against the job you believe you are hired for
steps: List the most critical details that must be included in the job spec for your target job.
Identify the obstacles that currently get in customers' way while they try to make progress.
Check whether current solutions address every one of those details, not just the functional core.
Map the experiences of purchase and use customers actually have and compare them with what the job spec requires.
Define where to improve, and ask how the organization ensures the customer's job guides product development, marketing and customer service decisions.
Check whether the functions involved in the customer's experience support the job in a coordinated way or whether they conflict.
caveats: These are diagnostic questions from the source, not a validated scoring instrument.
Answers will be organization-specific; the exercise is meant to surface misalignment, not produce a benchmark.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx
